about: Phase 12 pilot (Ram, 2026-11-21): life cycles of the Mughal, Roman and Ottoman empires. Neutral kinds, descriptive titles, boundaries at milestone events.

mughal-empire.title: Babur's conquest of northern India
mughal-empire.description: Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and the Rajput confederacy at Khanwa a year later, establishing Mughal rule over the Delhi–Agra region.

mughal-empire.title: Humayun loses the empire and wins it back
mughal-empire.description: Babur's son Humayun is driven out by Sher Shah Suri, and for fifteen years the Sur dynasty, not the Mughals, rules northern India. Humayun returns with Persian help and retakes Delhi in 1555, dying months later.
mughal-empire.note: The Mughals ruled nothing in India from 1540 to 1555 (the Sur Empire span covers it); the title and description say so rather than calling it 'early instability'.

mughal-empire.title: Expansion and reorganisation under Akbar
mughal-empire.description: Akbar's conquests stretch the empire from Kabul to Bengal and into the Deccan. He builds a lasting administration of ranked officers and a land-revenue system, allies with Rajput rulers, and follows a policy of religious accommodation.

mughal-empire.title: Stable rule and great building under Jahangir and Shah Jahan
mughal-empire.description: A largely stable half-century in which court painting and architecture flourish: the Taj Mahal and the new capital at Delhi, Shahjahanabad, date from these years. The empire grows more slowly, and a costly attempt to win back Central Asia fails.
mughal-empire.note: 'Height' here means stability, wealth and court culture; the territorial peak came later, under Aurangzeb (next phase), so the two are kept apart as the brief asked.

mughal-empire.title: Aurangzeb's wars in the Deccan
mughal-empire.description: Aurangzeb annexes the Deccan sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda, bringing the empire to its greatest extent. Decades of campaigning against the Marathas, and revolts by Jats, Sikhs and some Rajputs, strain its army and finances.

mughal-empire.title: Regional powers break away
mughal-empire.description: After Aurangzeb's death, wars of succession weaken the throne. The governors of Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh become rulers in their own right while still acknowledging the emperor, and the Marathas push north.

mughal-empire.title: Invasions and the rise of the East India Company
mughal-empire.description: Nadir Shah of Persia sacks Delhi and carries off the Peacock Throne. Afghan invasions follow, and the East India Company wins Bengal at Plassey and Buxar, while the emperor controls little beyond Delhi.

mughal-empire.title: Emperors in name, under Maratha and then British power
mughal-empire.description: The Company takes over Bengal's revenues, and the emperors keep their title and court in Delhi under Maratha and then, from 1803, British protection. After the 1857 rebellion, in which he was named its leader, the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, is exiled to Burma.
mughal-empire.note: The span ends at 1857 by convention; Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled in 1858.

roman-empire.title: Augustus creates the imperial system
roman-empire.description: After decades of civil war, Octavian takes the name Augustus and rules as the first emperor while keeping the outward forms of the Republic. He creates a standing army, reorganises the provinces and begins the long Pax Romana.

roman-empire.title: Julio-Claudian and Flavian emperors
roman-empire.description: Power passes within a few families, through murders and one year of civil war in which four emperors rule. The system survives these crises; Britain is conquered, and the Colosseum is built.
roman-empire.note: No milestone event exists for 14 (Augustus's death) or 96 (Nerva's accession); none drafted, since both are minor as quiz events. The 'year of four emperors' is 69.

roman-empire.title: The Nerva–Antonine emperors
roman-empire.description: Emperors chosen by adoption rather than birth rule for most of a century of internal stability. Trajan's conquests bring the empire to its greatest extent; Hadrian then fixes and fortifies its frontiers.
roman-empire.note: The source document called this 'Golden age / Pax Romana 96–180'. The Pax Romana is conventionally 27 BCE–180 CE (its own span); 96–180 is the Nerva–Antonine period, the 'Five Good Emperors' (Machiavelli's and Gibbon's label, avoided here).

roman-empire.title: The Severans and a growing army state
roman-empire.description: Commodus's misrule ends in his murder and a civil war won by Septimius Severus, whose dynasty relies heavily on the army. Citizenship is extended to nearly all free people of the empire, and pressure grows on the frontiers.

roman-empire.title: The crisis of civil wars, invasions and plague
roman-empire.description: Some two dozen emperors claim power in fifty years. Invasions, plague and a collapsing currency follow, and for a time the Gallic and Palmyrene empires break away, until Aurelian reunites the empire.

roman-empire.title: Diocletian, Constantine and a reorganised empire
roman-empire.description: Diocletian shares power among co-emperors and rebuilds the army, taxes and provinces. Constantine ends the persecution of Christians and founds Constantinople as a new capital, and Christianity becomes the state religion under Theodosius.

roman-empire.title: The Western empire breaks up
roman-empire.description: After Theodosius's death the empire is permanently ruled as two halves. The West loses its provinces to Goths, Vandals and Franks, Rome is sacked twice, and the last Western emperor is deposed. The East carries on, ruled from Constantinople.
roman-empire.note: Rome's span ends at 476; the Eastern continuation is the Byzantine Empire span (330–1453), linked as 'evolved into' in the milestones batch.

ottoman-empire.title: Osman's frontier principality
ottoman-empire.description: Osman leads one of several small Turkish principalities on the Byzantine frontier in northwest Anatolia, raiding and taking Byzantine towns.
ottoman-empire.note: 1299 is a traditional date, not a recorded event, so this phase is approximate. The Ottoman Empire span itself (1299–1922) is not marked approximate; it probably should be (c. 1299). Ram to decide.

ottoman-empire.title: Expansion into Anatolia and the Balkans
ottoman-empire.description: From Bursa the Ottomans spread across Anatolia and cross into Europe, defeating the Serbs at Kosovo. A crushing defeat by Timur at Ankara and a decade of civil war nearly end the state before it recovers.

ottoman-empire.title: Constantinople and the conquest of the Arab lands
ottoman-empire.description: Mehmed II makes Constantinople, now Istanbul, his capital. Selim I defeats the Safavids of Persia and the Mamluks, taking Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia.

ottoman-empire.title: Suleiman's reign
ottoman-empire.description: Suleiman takes Belgrade, Rhodes and most of Hungary, besieges Vienna and dominates the eastern Mediterranean. His law codes and the mosques of his architect Sinan make the reign a high point of Ottoman government and culture.

ottoman-empire.title: A changing empire, still a great power
ottoman-empire.description: Sultans rule less from the battlefield and more through viziers and the court, and the army and finances are remade. The empire stays a great power: it rebuilds its fleet after Lepanto, takes Crete, and under the Köprülü viziers reaches its largest extent in Europe.
ottoman-empire.note: No milestone event for 1566 (Suleiman's death); his accession event's text covers it. Historians now call this period a transformation rather than the start of decline (e.g. Tezcan, 'The Second Ottoman Empire').

ottoman-empire.title: Wars with the Habsburgs and Russia
ottoman-empire.description: Defeat at Vienna is followed by the loss of Hungary at Karlowitz. It is not a steady decline: the Ottomans win back Belgrade, but Russia's victories take the northern Black Sea coast, and Crimea is annexed by Russia.
ottoman-empire.note: Kept as 'contraction' (land lost), not 'decline': the empire also won wars in this period (Pruth 1711, Belgrade 1739).

ottoman-empire.title: Reform and the rise of nationalism
ottoman-empire.description: Selim III and Mahmud II rebuild the army, abolishing the Janissaries, and the Tanzimat reforms promise equal rights to all subjects, leading to a constitution. Meanwhile Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria break away, and European powers intervene.
ottoman-empire.note: The source document gave 1792; Selim III's reign, and his reforms' first steps, begin in 1789.

ottoman-empire.title: World war and the end of the sultanate
ottoman-empire.description: Allied with Germany, the empire wins at Gallipoli but loses its Arab lands; the war years see the Armenian genocide. Defeat brings occupation and the Turkish War of Independence, and the sultanate is abolished.
